e.etymology: A respelling of Peyton or Payton, an English surname from a place name: an Old English personal name, Paega, plus tun, farm or village.

A Biblical name, borne by Heber the Kenite, husband of Jael, from a Hebrew word for company or fellowship. It is also an English form of Irish Eibhear, and Latter-day Saints know it from church leaders Heber C. Kimball and Heber J. Grant.
From Persian rowshan, bright or luminous. The name spread with Persian across South Asia and is now common in India, Pakistan, Nepal and Sri Lanka; Roshni is the usual feminine counterpart.
The South Slavic form of Helen, common in Serbia and Croatia, from Greek Helene through Latin Helena. Helen is often linked to a Greek word for torch or light.
namesakes: Jelena Jankovic (Serbian tennis player, former world No. 1)

assoc.t: fan nickname for Justin Bieber and Selena Gomez as a couple

e.etymology: A Finnish name taken from Sami Aile in the late 1800s, usually explained as a form of Helga, holy or blessed. It reached the US with Finnish immigrants, and is also used as a spelling of Scottish Eilidh.
Of unclear origin as a given name. US use peaked in 2012, when actor Avan Jogia was starring in Nickelodeon's Victorious.
namesakes: Avan Jogia (actor, Beck on Nickelodeon's Victorious)

e.etymology: A respelling of Mason, an English occupational surname for a stoneworker, from Old French macon.
From Hebrew Amatsyahu, the Lord is strong. In the Old Testament Amaziah was a king of Judah, the son of Joash.
A short form in the family of Adalia, Adaline and Adelaide, whose Germanic root adal means noble. This spelling is used mostly in Spanish-speaking families.
A modern American coinage, a spelling in the family of Jamir and Jamere that pairs the popular Ja- beginning with the sound of Amir.
A Yiddish pet form of Chava, the Hebrew name of Eve, from a root meaning to live. It is used mainly in Orthodox Jewish communities.
e.note: The Ch is the throaty sound of Chanukah; others may read it CHAV-ee, and chavvy is a British slang insult.

e.meaning: my God is the Lord (Elias) or God is my oath (Elisabeth)
e.etymology: In Swedish a male variant of Elias; in Estonian and Brazilian use a female short form of Elisabeth; in Welsh the native spelling of Ellis. All go back to Hebrew names from the Bible.
A Swiss German occupational surname, a variant of Suter, from Latin sutor, shoemaker. Americans know it from John Sutter, on whose California land the gold of 1848 was found.
namesakes: John Sutter (pioneer whose sawmill set off the California Gold Rush)

e.etymology: From Hebrew Adayah, the Lord has adorned. Several men in the Old Testament bear the name, among them the grandfather of King Josiah; in the US it is now given mostly to girls.
A respelling of Kinsley, an English surname from a Yorkshire place name: the clearing of a man called Cyne, a short name built on Old English cyne, royal.
A Hebrew name from the Old Testament, where Azel is a descendant of King Saul through Jonathan. It is explained as noble or reserved, and was in use in 19th-century America.
The French form of a Breton name, the feminine of Mael, from a Breton word for prince or chief. It has been popular in France since the 1990s.
From Sanskrit shloka, the couplet verse form of the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and many Hindu prayers. As a name it carries the sense of a sacred verse.
The Latin form of Greek Aias, of uncertain root. Two heroes of the Trojan War carry it in Homer's Iliad: Ajax the Great, son of Telamon, and the swift Ajax the Lesser.
namesakes: Ajax the Great (Greek hero of Homer's Iliad)

assoc.t: Ajax scouring powder and dish soap
Greek hero of the Trojan War

e.etymology: A spelling of Lucas with a doubled c, seen especially in Brazil. Lucas is the Latin form of Greek Loukas, man from Lucania, a region of southern Italy, and the name of the Gospel writer Luke.
A respelling of Ensley, an English surname related to Ainsley and Ansley. Those come from place names ending in Old English leah, a woodland clearing.
Latin for female warrior, from bellum, war. It is the traditional name of a bright star in Orion, and J.K. Rowling gave it to the witch Bellatrix Lestrange.
e.note: Most people will think of Bellatrix Lestrange, the cruel Death Eater in Harry Potter.

e.etymology: The feminine form of Vihaan, from Sanskrit vihana, dawn or daybreak. Both names became popular with Indian families in the 2000s.
A short form of names that carry the sound, such as Isaiah, Zayden, Zaire and Xavier, now also given on its own.
In Persian, Ario or Aryo is a short form of Ariobarzan, the name of an ancient Persian general, built on the old Iranian word arya, noble. Ario is also a rare Italian name.
A respelling of Selah that spells out the SAY-luh pronunciation. Selah is a Hebrew word that closes many verses of the Psalms, thought to mark a pause or musical interlude.
A spelling of Katherine, from Greek Aikaterine, of uncertain origin. The h comes from an early link with Greek katharos, pure. Saint Catherine of Alexandria spread the name across Christian Europe.
namesakes: Katharine Graham (publisher of The Washington Post)

e.etymology: A modern American name of the 1990s, close in sound to Asia, Deja and Dasha. It has no settled source or meaning.
The Welsh spelling of Tristan, the knight who loves Iseult in medieval romance. The name goes back to Celtic Drystan, from drest, riot or tumult, and was later linked with French triste, sad.
An English place name and surname, from Old English denu, valley, and tun, settlement. It moved from surname to first name in the 1800s.
namesakes: Cy Young (Hall of Fame pitcher, born Denton True Young)

e.etymology: From Old Swedish Gotstaf, usually read as Old Norse Gautr, Geat, plus stafr, staff, though the origin is debated. It has been a Swedish royal name since Gustav Vasa in the 1500s.
namesakes: Gustav Klimt (Austrian painter of The Kiss)

e.etymology: A variant of Ariane, the French form of Greek Ariadne, usually read as most holy. In myth Ariadne gave Theseus the thread that led him out of the Minotaur's labyrinth.
